chapter.title: The bell that starts the line

cards.body: Tom's Friday sales report never sent. His laptop was asleep in his bag, but that was only half the reason. By the end of this chapter you'll know the whole story, and you can build your first working line in about 10 minutes. In n8n, think of a small assembly line: a bell rings, each station does one job, and the item rides the belt to the end. **Nothing moves until the bell rings**, and in n8n that bell is called the *trigger*.

cards.prompt: Your workflow has a Google Sheets node and a Gmail node, but no trigger. A new row lands in the sheet. What happens?

options.text: The Google Sheets node notices the new row and starts the line.
The Gmail node sends an email on its own.

whyNot.a: That's confusing a station with the bell: a Google Sheets node only reads the sheet once the line is already running. Watching for new rows is a trigger's job.
whyNot.c: That's confusing the end of the line with the start: the Gmail node only acts when an item reaches it, and with no bell, nothing ever does.

cards.reteach: A workflow stays asleep until its trigger fires. It doesn't matter that the stations are set up, or that something changed in the sheet. Without the bell, no station moves.

cards.title: Three common bells
cards.body:
A *trigger* is the first box in every n8n workflow. It's the event that wakes the workflow up. **No trigger, no run.**

There are more kinds of bell than this, but three common ones will take you a long way. A time on the clock, like every weekday at 8:30 (the *Schedule Trigger*). A form being filled in, like a holiday request (the *Form Trigger*). Or a change in another app, like a new row landing in a spreadsheet. Some apps ping n8n at a web address made for that workflow (a *webhook*); with others, like Google Sheets, n8n checks for anything new on a regular timer, which you can change.

To pick the bell, ask one question: what moment should start this?
cards.simpler: A trigger is the first box in every n8n workflow. It wakes the workflow up. **No trigger, no run.** There are more kinds of bell, but three common ones go a long way. A clock time, like every weekday at 8:30, is the Schedule Trigger. A filled-in form, like a holiday request, is the Form Trigger. A change in another app, like a new spreadsheet row, is the third. Some apps ping n8n at a web address made for that workflow, called a webhook. With others, like Google Sheets, n8n checks for new things on a regular timer. To choose, ask what moment should start this.

cards.title: Priya's Monday bell
cards.body: Priya forgets her timesheet every Monday. In n8n she clicks to add a first step and picks Schedule Trigger: every week, Monday, 8am. Next she adds one station, an Edit Fields node, with a field called message set to "Timesheet due by 5pm". She clicks Execute workflow. Both boxes turn green, and the output panel shows her sentence, waiting like a parcel at the end of the belt. **One bell, one station, one result you can see.**

The output panel shows her sentence, like a parcel waiting at the end of the belt. **One bell, one station, one result you can see.**

cards.prompt: Maya handles returns for a shoe shop. Every time a customer fills in the returns form, she wants the details logged. Which bell fits?

options.text: Maya clicks Execute workflow each morning

whyNot.a: That's a clock bell when this task needs an event bell: it rings whether or not anyone sent a return.
whyNot.c: That's testing by hand, not a bell: the line only runs on days Maya remembers.

cards.reteach: Ask what moment should start the line. Here it's "a customer submits the form", so the form itself is the bell. A clock suits tasks tied to a time. It doesn't suit tasks that start when someone does something.

cards.title: Ringing it by hand
cards.body:
You'd think a Schedule Trigger set to Monday 8am will ring on Monday. Not yet. **A schedule only rings by itself once the workflow is switched on**, and only while n8n is running somewhere: on n8n's cloud, or on a computer that's awake. Depending on your n8n version, the switch may be labelled Active or Publish.

Until then, you ring the bell yourself. Clicking Execute workflow runs the whole line once, right now, whatever the time. That's how you test: press it, watch the boxes go green, read what came out.

Switching it on for real comes in chapter 7. For now, ring it by hand.
cards.simpler: A Schedule Trigger set to Monday 8am won't ring on Monday yet. **A schedule only rings by itself once the workflow is switched on**, and only while n8n is running somewhere, on n8n's cloud or on a computer that's awake. The switch may say Active or Publish, depending on your n8n version. Until then, you ring it yourself. Clicking Execute workflow runs the whole line once, right now. That's how you test: press it, watch for green, read the result. Switching it on comes in chapter 7.

cards.body: Back to Tom. He builds a line that posts the weekly sales total every Friday at 4pm. He tests it by hand, sees green boxes, and goes home happy. Friday at 4:00 comes and goes in silence: he never switched the workflow on, and n8n was running on his laptop, which spent Friday asleep in his bag. The warning sign: if you've only ever seen it run when you clicked, it hasn't yet shown it can run on its own.
cards.simpler: Back to Tom. He builds a line that posts the weekly sales total every Friday at 4pm. He tests it by hand, sees green boxes, and goes home happy. Friday at 4:00 passes in silence. He never switched the workflow on, and n8n was running on his laptop, which spent Friday asleep in his bag. The warning sign: **if you've only seen it run when you clicked, it hasn't yet shown it can run on its own**.

cards.prompt: It's Wednesday, 14:10. Your workflow's Schedule Trigger is set to Monday 8am, and the workflow isn't switched on. You click Execute workflow. What happens?

options.text: The line runs once, right now.
It runs now, then every Monday on its own.

whyNot.b: That's confusing the bell ringing itself with you ringing it: a click runs the line straight away, whatever the schedule says.
whyNot.c: That's confusing switching the workflow on with testing it: one click is one run, and the Monday bell waits for the on switch.

cards.reteach: A bell can ring in two ways. You can ring it by hand with Execute workflow, which runs the line once, now. Or it rings itself at the set time, but only after the workflow is switched on.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every n8n workflow starts with a trigger, the bell that wakes the line: often a time, a form, or a change in another app. **Clicking Execute workflow rings it once by hand to test; it only rings by itself once you switch the workflow on.**
cards.simpler: Every n8n workflow starts with a trigger, the bell that wakes the line. It's often a time, a form, or a change in another app. **Clicking Execute workflow rings it once by hand to test; it only rings by itself once you switch the workflow on.**

cards.body:
Open n8n, either the cloud trial or your own install. Add a Schedule Trigger and one Edit Fields node holding a message for yourself, then click Execute workflow. Two green boxes means your first line works.

Tomorrow: click into that first green box. Your bell handed the next station more than a ding, and you'll learn to read it.
cards.simpler: Open n8n, either the cloud trial or your own install. Add a Schedule Trigger. Then add one Edit Fields node with a message for yourself. Click Execute workflow. If you see **two green boxes, your first line works**. Think of it as pressing the bell once to hear it ring. Tomorrow: click into that first green box. Your bell passed along more than a ding, and you'll learn to read it.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now build a workflow that starts on a schedule and run it by hand to watch it work.

dubious_claims: Calling a webhook a 'private web address' is misleading. Anyone who has the link can reach it, because it is a hard-to-guess public link, not a private one.
'n8n checks every few minutes' for Google Sheets is loose. The Google Sheets Trigger checks every minute by default, and you can change that.

Card 1 says Tom's report failed because 'his laptop was asleep', but card 7 shows he also never switched the workflow on, so it would have failed even with the laptop awake. The hook gives only half the cause.
repairedFrom.why: The first exercise only tests the assembly-line metaphor, not n8n, so the answer is obvious and the card adds nothing a reader can use.
repairedFrom.fix: Rewrite card 2 as an n8n question: 'Your workflow has a Google Sheets node and a Gmail node but no trigger. A new row lands in the sheet. What happens?' Keep 'nothing runs' as the right answer.
